agenda: Map Rafael Mendes's dispatch day at Harbor Logistics and identify where Kestrel Dispatch saves time.
Examine bulk import and reporting friction with concrete examples.
Test demand and willingness to pay for proactive delay alerts and an API.
Agree follow-ups and close the interview without promising an unplanned release.

chapters.title: A Day in Harbor Dispatch
beats: Amara asks Rafael to walk through a 6 a.m. shift with 68 trucks and roughly 110 stops.
Rafael explains how the live map and auto-assign reduce morning phone calls and where human dispatchers still intervene.

chapters.title: Imports and Reports
beats: Rafael describes a 420-row Monday import, 17 rejected rows, and weak error messages.
Amara tests whether a preview and row-level fixes would beat a complete importer redesign.
Rafael compares the slow weekly report with a dispatcher-built spreadsheet.

chapters.title: Delay Alerts and API Demand
beats: Rafael describes a missed delay that reached the customer before Harbor's dispatcher and says a useful alert must arrive before the commitment window.
Amara tests a monthly premium for proactive alerts and asks how Harbor would use an API.
Rafael distinguishes useful export access from competitor sales claims.

chapters.title: Priority and Follow-up
beats: Rafael ranks import preview above reports, delay alerts, and API access for immediate impact while separating willingness to pay from urgency.
Amara commits to specific research follow-ups; Rafael agrees to share a redacted file and review alert wording.
Both recap what is known, what remains unpromised, and close the call.
